title: Widespread Body Aches - Fibromyalgia (with Polymyalgia Rheumatica / GCA Reasoning)
patient_instructions: You are Sandra Fitzgerald, a 50-year-old woman, presenting to your GP with aches and pains 'all over my body' for about eight months. You are frustrated: you have seen several doctors who told you 'nothing is wrong' and that your blood tests were normal. The pain is in your neck, shoulders, back, chest wall, hips and limbs - it feels like it is in the muscles rather than in specific swollen joints. There is some general stiffness in the mornings that eases as you get going, but no single hot, red or swollen joint. You are exhausted, sleep poorly (you wake through the night unrefreshed), and struggle to concentrate ('foggy'). You have NO weight loss, NO fevers or night sweats, NO new severe headache, NO scalp tenderness, NO jaw pain when chewing and NO visual disturbance. No rashes, no cold intolerance/constipation, no recent diarrhoea or travel, not on a statin or any regular medication. Mood has been low with the ongoing pain but you have no thoughts of self-harm. You live with a supportive partner and work part-time. IDEAS: you fear you have 'something serious that keeps getting missed'. CONCERNS: not being believed and never getting better. EXPECTATIONS: a real explanation and a plan. Affect: initially frustrated and slightly defensive; softens if the doctor validates that the pain is real. Volunteer red-flag answers as negative only when specifically asked.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in an Australian general practice. Sandra Fitzgerald, a 50-year-old woman, presents with widespread aches and pains. Her ESR and CRP are normal. In this 8-minute station: take a focused history (about 6 minutes) that safely narrows a broad differential, then examination findings will appear - she looks well, with soft-tissue tenderness at multiple sites but no joint swelling, redness or deformity and normal power. Explain your most likely diagnosis and the key differentials to the patient, and outline an initial management plan. You do not need to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: This is a demanding exclusion-based reasoning station. Reward a systematic widespread-pain history that screens the major mimics: inflammatory arthritis (RA), polymyalgia rheumatica, SLE/connective-tissue disease, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia, statin myopathy, infection (hepatitis, post-viral, travel), malignancy (leukaemia/lymphoma) and mood/somatic symptom disorder. The candidate must have a clear red-flag 'escape hatch': weight loss, fever/night sweats, bone pain, focal neurology or raised inflammatory markers should redirect away from a fibromyalgia label. Critically, in an older patient the shoulder/hip-girdle-pain variant is polymyalgia rheumatica - the candidate must screen for giant cell (temporal) arteritis (new headache, scalp/temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms) because GCA is a SIGHT-THREATENING emergency needing urgent high-dose corticosteroids. Ensure the candidate does NOT describe PMR as a blood-vessel vasculitis or as identical to GCA. For fibromyalgia management, expect non-drug therapy first (graded aerobic exercise, CBT, sleep hygiene) with low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine or pregabalin as options. Prompt if needed: 'What must you not miss in an older patient with girdle pain?'

criteria: Structured pain history (muscles vs joints, sites/four quadrants, duration, pattern, sleep, fatigue, cognitive 'fog', functional and mood impact)
Systematic differential-based screen: inflammatory arthritis, PMR, SLE/CTD, thyroid, hypercalcaemia, statin, infection/travel, malignancy
Explicit red-flag screen (weight loss, fever/night sweats, bone pain, focal neurology) as the escape hatch before labelling fibromyalgia
Screens for GCA features (new headache, scalp/temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms) and mood/self-harm sensitively
Gives fibromyalgia as most likely - a clinical, exclusion-based, symptom diagnosis with normal inflammatory markers and no structural damage
Correctly frames PMR as bilateral shoulder/hip-girdle inflammatory pain and stiffness (not a large-vessel vasculitis) that is associated with but distinct from GCA
Recognises normal ESR/CRP argue against PMR/inflammatory disease and selects targeted confirmatory tests (TSH, CK, calcium, RF/anti-CCP, ANA) to exclude mimics
States suspected GCA is a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate high-dose corticosteroids and urgent referral before biopsy
Fibromyalgia management: non-pharmacological cornerstone (graded aerobic exercise, CBT, sleep hygiene) as first-line
Appropriate pharmacological options (low-dose amitriptyline at night, or duloxetine/pregabalin) and pain-service referral where indicated
Validates that the pain is real, avoids dismissiveness, and explores the patient's frustration and ideas/concerns/expectations
Gives a clear, hopeful lay explanation and agrees a shared, function-focused plan

red_flags: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis - new headache, scalp/temporal tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms: a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate high-dose corticosteroids
Constitutional features (unintentional weight loss, fever, night sweats, bone pain) suggesting malignancy (leukaemia/lymphoma) or infection
Markedly raised inflammatory markers or new focal neurology - redirect away from a fibromyalgia label toward inflammatory, malignant or neurological disease
Low mood with any suicidal ideation in a patient with chronic pain and repeated non-diagnosis
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines, Australia) - fibromyalgia: non-drug therapy (graded aerobic exercise, CBT, sleep hygiene) is the cornerstone; low-dose amitriptyline at night, duloxetine or pregabalin are recommended pharmacological options
eTG / RACGP - suspected giant cell arteritis requires immediate high-dose oral prednis(ol)one and urgent referral before temporal artery biopsy to prevent irreversible visual loss

Murtagh/Australian practice - polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder/hip-girdle pain, morning stiffness, age >50) has a characteristically very high ESR (>50 mm/hr) and responds rapidly to low-dose prednis(ol)one (~15 mg daily)
RACGP - a normal ESR/CRP makes PMR and active inflammatory arthritis unlikely; use targeted tests (TSH, CK, calcium, RF/anti-CCP, ANA) to exclude mimics before a fibromyalgia diagnosis
learning_objectives: Approach chronic widespread pain as an exclusion-based diagnosis with a structured mimic screen and clear red-flag escape hatch
Distinguish fibromyalgia (normal markers, no structural damage) from PMR and inflammatory disease
Correctly conceptualise PMR versus giant cell arteritis and recognise GCA as a sight-threatening emergency
Construct an evidence-based fibromyalgia plan led by non-pharmacological therapy with appropriate Australian medication options
key_points: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis of widespread pain (all four quadrants, >3 months) with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive 'fog'; no confirmatory biomarker and normal inflammatory markers
PMR is peri-articular/bursal and synovial inflammation of the shoulder and hip girdles - NOT a blood-vessel vasculitis and NOT synonymous with GCA
Every PMR patient must be screened for GCA; suspected GCA gets immediate high-dose steroids and urgent referral before biopsy
Manage fibromyalgia with exercise, CBT and sleep hygiene first; amitriptyline, duloxetine or pregabalin are options and the goal is improved function, not being pain-free

citations.claim: Polymyalgia rheumatica presents with shoulder- and hip-girdle pain and morning stiffness in patients over 50 and must be screened alongside temporal arteritis (new headache, visual symptoms, jaw claudication, temporal artery tenderness), with a characteristically very high ESR (>50 mm/hr).
Fibromyalgia is defined by a history of widespread pain affecting all four body quadrants (neck to low back), supporting a symptom-based diagnosis once other causes are excluded.
The differential for widespread musculoskeletal pain includes the often-missed pitfalls of fibromyalgia syndrome, polymyalgia rheumatica and crystal arthropathies alongside connective-tissue disease.
